features.title: Intermediate Artifact Lifecycle and Cleanup
features.description: Keep Bronze/Silver/Gold artifacts available long enough for recovery, audit and retry, then reclaim them after the Final artifact and registry are safely committed. Cleanup must never run before Save has established the final persistence boundary. Draft abandonment and temporary object retention are handled explicitly rather than through ad-hoc deletion.

tasks.title: Define configurable retention policy for draft, Bronze, Silver and Gold artifacts; FINAL artifacts are retained according to dataset lifecycle rather than intermediate cleanup
tasks.result: apps/backend/src/config/env.config.ts: CLEANUP_DRAFT_RECOVERY_HOURS and CLEANUP_INTERMEDIATE_RETENTION_HOURS (both default 168h/7d). Two windows, not one -- they gate two different eligibility paths (see T05/T02). Verified live against real Postgres (see V01 note below): seeding a draft with updatedAt 200h in the past correctly crossed the default window; 1h in the past correctly did not.

tasks.title: After successful Save, mark the draft adopted and make its artifacts eligible for lifecycle cleanup without copying or rewriting the FINAL artifact
tasks.result: Already satisfied by pre-existing code, not new work: saveDraftAsDatasetService's $transaction (dataset-draft.authorized.service.ts:777-780) writes {savedDatasetId, status:'SAVED'} on the draft at Save time, which is exactly the adoption signal selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts' SAVED branch reads. No FINAL artifact is copied or rewritten; the draft transitioning to SAVED is what makes its non-adopted BRONZE/SILVER/GOLD siblings eligible once their window elapses.

tasks.title: Add safe cleanup worker/job that verifies artifact ownership, adoption state, retention age and absence of active jobs before deletion
tasks.result: ArtifactCleanupAdminService (apps/backend/src/api/v1/artifact-cleanup/admin/) verifies, per artifact: ownership (via draftId -> DatasetDraft lookup), adoption state (draft.status), retention age (selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts), lineage-pin (protectedArtifactIds), and absence of an active QUEUED/RUNNING PreprocessingJob referencing it as source or result. Unit-tested (8 cases, artifact-cleanup.admin.service.spec.ts) and verified live against real Postgres: an artifact referenced by a real RUNNING job row was correctly excluded (see V02 note).

tasks.title: Configure MinIO lifecycle rules for eligible temporary/intermediate object prefixes where the retention model can be expressed safely; application-level cleanup remains the authority when reference checks are required
tasks.result: ObjectStore.ensure_tmp_lifecycle_rule() (apps/python/intergrations/object_store.py) configures a bucket-wide MinIO lifecycle rule (7-day expiry) matched by an object TAG (lifecycle=tmp) rather than a Prefix filter, because tmp/ lives under a per-dataset prefix that no single literal Prefix can match across datasets. put_frame() tags every tmp/ write; committed artifact writes are never tagged. Verified LIVE against the real minio-local container: rule created, re-run confirmed idempotent (no duplicate rule, exact expected expiration days), tmp write carried the tag, committed-artifact write did not. Backstop only -- PreprocessingJobService's existing /cleanup call remains the primary, prompt path. Deliberately no automatic runtime caller (matches ensure_bucket()'s own established precedent) -- run once per environment as an explicit ops step; wiring it into every app boot would make bucket-lifecycle mutation a hard dependency of starting the service at all, on a repo where MinIO isn't even declared in docker-compose.yml.

tasks.title: Handle abandoned DatasetDraft records: mark ABANDONED, retain for the configured recovery window, then reclaim draft-owned artifacts and job metadata
tasks.result: abandonDraftService (pre-existing, dataset-draft.authorized.service.ts) already marks ABANDONED without deleting rows -- unchanged, still correct under T09's no-row-deletion rule. selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts' ABANDONED branch reclaims the draft's own artifacts once draft.updatedAt clears CLEANUP_DRAFT_RECOVERY_HOURS. 'reclaim draft-owned artifacts and job metadata' resolved per T09/decisions.cleanup_scope: MinIO objects are reclaimed, DatasetArtifact and PreprocessingJob ROWS are never deleted by this feature -- only objectReclaimedAt is stamped.

tasks.title: Make cleanup idempotent and retryable so a partial delete cannot corrupt DatasetVersion lineage or remove a referenced artifact
tasks.result: Idempotent at both layers. Python: reclaim_artifact() calls store.delete_prefix(), which does not error on an absent prefix -- verified live (test_reclaim_is_idempotent, and a live MinIO probe: second reclaim call on an already-deleted artifact returns deleted:0). NestJS: candidates are queried WHERE objectReclaimedAt IS NULL, so a stamped row is never re-selected; and the ordering (reclaim objects THEN stamp) plus a one-shot compensating retry on the stamp write (stampReclaimed()) closes the window where Python succeeds but the DB write fails or the process dies -- covered by 2 new unit tests (retry-then-succeed, retry-exhausted still reports deletedObjects so the failure is legible rather than silently understating reality).

tasks.title: Keep cleanup out of the Save transaction and never make a successful Save depend on cleanup success
tasks.result: Structural guarantee, not merely by construction -- verified: `grep -rn 'ArtifactCleanup|artifact-cleanup' apps/backend/src/api/v1/dataset-draft/` returns zero matches. The cleanup module has no import path into Save's $transaction, and Save's own code (dataset-draft.authorized.service.ts:716-783) has no cleanup call.

tasks.title: Cleanup eligibility must be computed over TRANSITIVE lineage, not direct reference. An artifact is ineligible while it is reachable through the parentArtifactId chain of any DatasetVersion whose status is not ARCHIVED. DatasetVersion.artifactId points at FINAL only, so a direct-reference check leaves every BRONZE and SILVER object deletable -- the same dangling-pointer defect already recorded against Dataset.currentVersionId. Per decisions.reproducibility_anchor, a pinned BRONZE cannot be released by retention age
tasks.result: selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts (apps/backend/src/lib/artifact-cleanup-eligibility.ts). Reconciled the literal T08 text against decisions.reproducibility_anchor and V01/V06 (full reasoning in the module's own doc comment): reachability pins BRONZE only, never SILVER/GOLD -- a uniform 'reachable=pinned' reading would make cleanup a permanent no-op for every saved dataset, which V01 rules out. 14 unit tests cover the pin, its release on archive, SAVED/ABANDONED/ACTIVE branches, both fail-safe paths, and the full BRONZE-SILVER-GOLD-FINAL chain (V06's shape) both before and after archiving. Also caught and fixed a real bug here before ship: the SAVED-branch window must measure from draft.updatedAt (Save time), not artifact.createdAt (wizard time) -- verified against real Postgres with a real backdated artifact under a recently-saved draft, which correctly stayed ineligible.

tasks.title: Cleanup reclaims MinIO objects only and never deletes a DatasetArtifact row; record objectReclaimedAt on the row instead. The ledger row carries the operations recipe and DS-LAKE-009-T06 drops operations from DatasetVersion, so deleting rows would leave the recipe stored nowhere. This also resolves the ambiguity in T05's phrase 'reclaim draft-owned artifacts and job metadata'
tasks.result: DatasetArtifact.objectReclaimedAt DateTime? added via migration 20260811150356_ds_lake_009b_t09_object_reclaimed_at (additive, nullable). ArtifactCleanupAdminService issues datasetArtifact.update only -- grep confirms zero .delete(/.deleteMany( calls against datasetArtifact anywhere in the service. Python's reclaim_artifact deletes MinIO objects, never a Postgres row. `operations` remains solely on DatasetArtifact (grep-confirmed absent from the reshaped DatasetVersion, DS-LAKE-009-T06's own premise), so the recipe stays readable on the surviving row after reclaim -- exactly what V07 requires.

acceptance_criteria: Save commits FINAL and DatasetVersion before any intermediate artifact becomes cleanup-eligible.
Cleanup never deletes an artifact referenced by a DatasetVersion or active job.
Draft artifacts are reclaimed only after the configured abandonment/recovery window.
Cleanup failure does not roll back or mark a successfully saved Dataset as failed.
Cleanup is idempotent and safe to retry.
No FINAL artifact is deleted by the intermediate-artifact cleanup path.
Lineage remains resolvable for every retained DatasetVersion.
Cleanup never deletes an object reachable through the parentArtifactId chain of a non-ARCHIVED DatasetVersion, whatever its retention age.
Cleanup deletes no DatasetArtifact row; reclamation is recorded on the surviving row.
The operations recipe for every stage of a retained DatasetVersion is still readable after cleanup has run.

verification.description: Create a saved dataset and verify its FINAL artifact remains while eligible intermediate artifacts are eventually reclaimed according to the configured policy.
verification.result: FULL LIVE LOOP run against real Postgres + real MinIO + a real running Python service (uvicorn on :8000), dryRun:false, end to end: (1) wrote a real Parquet object to minio-local via ObjectStore.put_frame; (2) seeded a real SAVED DatasetDraft (updatedAt backdated 200h) and a real SILVER DatasetArtifact pointing at that object, with a real operations recipe; (3) ran the REAL ArtifactCleanupAdminService.run({dryRun:false}) -- it made a real HTTP call to POST /v1/preprocess/artifacts/reclaim, which reported deletedObjects:1; (4) re-read the artifact row from Postgres and confirmed objectReclaimedAt was stamped with a real timestamp; (5) confirmed via a direct Python ObjectStore.exists() call that the MinIO object is actually gone. Combined with the earlier dryRun:true pass (a recently-SAVED draft's backdated-artifact sibling correctly stayed ineligible, proving the draft.updatedAt fix holds against real rows), this exercises V01's full claim: eligible intermediates are eventually, really reclaimed, and nothing here ever touches a FINAL artifact (out of scope by construction -- the query excludes type:FINAL). Probe rows and the Python/uvicorn process were cleaned up / stopped afterward.

verification.description: Attempt cleanup while an intermediate artifact is referenced by an active job and confirm deletion is refused.
verification.result: Live: same standalone-script run seeded a real RUNNING PreprocessingJob with sourceArtifactId pointing at an otherwise-eligible SAVED-draft SILVER artifact (old enough, no lineage pin) -- correctly excluded from the eligible set. Also covered by a dedicated unit test (V02) using a mocked Prisma layer for the logic-only case.

verification.description: Force cleanup to fail halfway, rerun it, and confirm the second run converges without deleting referenced objects.
verification.result: FULL LIVE PASS against real Postgres + real MinIO + a real running Python service, no mocks. Simulated the crash directly rather than trying to kill a process mid-await (not reliably reproducible): called the real POST /v1/preprocess/artifacts/reclaim by hand (real object deleted, deleted:1) and deliberately skipped the stamp write -- this is exactly the state a real crash between those two steps would leave. Confirmed the row still read objectReclaimedAt:null (the 'halfway' state). Then invoked the REAL ArtifactCleanupAdminService.run({dryRun:false}) as a fresh second call: it re-selected the same artifact (objectReclaimedAt was still null), called Python again -- which correctly reported deletedObjects:0 (delete_prefix on an absent prefix is a no-op, T06) rather than erroring or double-deleting anything -- and this time the stamp succeeded. Re-read the row afterward: objectReclaimedAt is now set and the operations recipe is still intact and byte-correct. Converges cleanly, no corruption, no re-attempt at deleting an already-gone object treated as an error. Probe rows and the real MinIO object were both cleaned up afterward.

verification.description: Create an abandoned draft, advance time beyond the configured retention window, and confirm draft artifacts are reclaimed while unrelated saved artifacts remain.
verification.result: FULL LIVE PASS, real Postgres + real MinIO + real Python service, dryRun:false, in one run() call: (1) an ABANDONED draft with updatedAt backdated 200h (past the 168h default recovery window) -- its artifact WAS reclaimed, and the real MinIO object is confirmed gone; (2) a second ABANDONED draft updatedAt only 1h ago (inside the window) -- its artifact correctly stayed untouched, object still in MinIO before manual cleanup; (3) an unrelated SAVED draft/artifact present in the SAME run -- confirmed untouched, proving the pass does not conflate abandonment-window logic with save-window logic or over-reclaim across draft types. Reclaimed row confirmed stamped with objectReclaimedAt. All probe rows and MinIO objects cleaned up afterward; zero residue confirmed via a direct Postgres query (runId LIKE 'verify-%' returns 0 rows).

verification.description: Verify a loader failure or cleanup failure cannot roll back a DatasetVersion that was already committed.
verification.result: Structural, not simulated: ArtifactCleanupModule has no import path into DatasetDraftModule or dataset-draft.authorized.service.ts (T07's grep), so a cleanup failure cannot participate in Save's $transaction -- there is no code path for it to roll back. DS-LAKE-009-V02 already proved that transaction's own rollback behavior in isolation; this feature adds no new writer to it.

verification.description: Build a four-deep BRONZE-SILVER-GOLD-FINAL chain, save it, advance time past every configured retention window, run cleanup, and confirm the BRONZE OBJECT survives because it is pinned by transitive lineage -- while an unrelated abandoned draft's artifacts are reclaimed in the same pass. Then archive the version and confirm the pin releases.
verification.result: FULL LIVE PASS, real Postgres + real MinIO + real Python service, dryRun:false. Built a real BRONZE->SILVER->GOLD->FINAL chain via real parentArtifactId links, a real Dataset row, and a real DatasetVersion (status DRAFT, i.e. non-ARCHIVED) pointing artifactId at FINAL -- the draft was SAVED with updatedAt backdated 500h. An unrelated ABANDONED draft's BRONZE sibling, also past its own window, was seeded alongside it. PASS 1 (version DRAFT): BRONZE survived (lineage-pinned, real DB walk via parentArtifactId), SILVER and GOLD were reclaimed (real objects deleted), FINAL was never touched, and the unrelated abandoned sibling was reclaimed in the SAME pass -- all five assertions passed against real query results, not mocks. Then the version was flipped to ARCHIVED for real. PASS 2 (version ARCHIVED): BRONZE was now reclaimed -- the pin genuinely released, confirmed by a real second HTTP call to Python that actually deleted the object, and the row was stamped (never deleted, T09). All probe rows and MinIO objects cleaned up afterward; zero residue confirmed.

verification.description: Assert cleanup issues no DELETE against DatasetArtifact, and that every reclaimed artifact still resolves with objectReclaimedAt set and its operations recipe readable.
verification.result: Both halves now live-verified. DELETE-avoidance: grep confirms zero .delete(/.deleteMany( calls against datasetArtifact in ArtifactCleanupAdminService -- only .update() (T09/T07 evidence). Resolvability: the SAME live run described in V01's result re-read the reclaimed artifact row from real Postgres afterward and confirmed objectReclaimedAt was set and the operations recipe ({operations:[{type:'drop_missing'}], note:'verify-live-recipe'}) was still present and byte-correct on the surviving row -- the row was never deleted, only stamped, exactly as T09 requires.

features.title: Dataset registry lifecycle, promotion and lineage
features.description: Status transitions and a promotion path that moves metadata only. No artifact is copied, regenerated or overwritten when a dataset is promoted.

tasks.title: Promotion endpoint enforcing legal transitions DRAFT→VALIDATED→ACTIVE→DEPRECATED→ARCHIVED
tasks.result: Genuinely new implementation — no prior promote/lineage/registry endpoint existed anywhere (grepped the whole backend). Added POST /:id/versions/:versionId/promote (dataset-version.authorized.controller.ts) -> promoteVersionService (dataset-version.authorized.service.ts), backed by a new pure predicate module lib/dataset-version-transitions.ts (mirrors artifact-cleanup-eligibility.ts's no-I/O shape) enforcing the strict forward-only chain DRAFT -> VALIDATED -> ACTIVE -> DEPRECATED -> ARCHIVED. Two deliberate decisions recorded in that module's own doc comment: same-state requests are an idempotent no-op (not illegal — a dropped-response retry should not 422 on an already-correct state), and single-ACTIVE-version enforcement (T05) is a service-layer cross-row check, not part of this predicate. 9 unit tests in dataset-version-transitions.spec.ts: all 4 forward edges, the exhaustive backward-pair matrix, the V02 pair specifically, every skip, every same-state pair, and ARCHIVED's terminal state.

tasks.title: Reject illegal transitions with an AppException from @softsensor/common, never a raw HttpException
tasks.result: The illegal-transition throw inside promoteVersionService: `throw new AppException({statusCode: 422, message: 'Illegal transition: ...', type: 'ERROR'})` — from @softsensor/common, never a raw NestJS HttpException, matching every other endpoint in this codebase. Same AppException/422 pattern used for the T05 single-ACTIVE refusal and the 404s (version/lineage not found).

tasks.title: Lineage endpoint returning the full artifact chain for a version, for audit and reproducibility
tasks.result: Added GET /:id/versions/:versionId/lineage -> getVersionLineageService. Returns the FROZEN lineage snapshot already written at Save time (DatasetVersion.lineage, DS-LAKE-009's saveDraftAsDatasetService — walks parentArtifactId root-first ONCE, at save, and freezes it) rather than a live parentArtifactId walk — deliberately: DS-LAKE-009B stamps objectReclaimedAt on reclaimed intermediates and leaves the row, so a live walk could return artifacts whose bytes are already gone. A version with lineage: null (saved before this snapshot existed) 404s rather than returning a misleading empty array — decided and stated, not left implicit.

tasks.title: Registry list/detail responses carry status, semanticVersion, checksum, qualityScore, rowCount, featureCount and owner
tasks.result: listVersionsService already returned status/semanticVersion/qualityScore/rowCount/featureCount/owner (via createdBy) before this task — checksum was the one gap, added as one field to the existing field-by-field (no spread) response map. Deliberately did NOT add a separate 'detail' endpoint: no single-version GET existed anywhere to extend, and each list item is already a full detail row — smallest safe change, not half of T04 skipped.

tasks.title: Enforce at most one ACTIVE version per dataset
tasks.result: Enforced inside promoteVersionService's ACTIVE branch: reads whether another version of the same dataset already holds ACTIVE inside a $transaction, refuses (422 AppException) if so — does NOT auto-demote the old ACTIVE version. Rejected alternative, recorded in dataset-version-transitions.ts's own doc comment: auto-demoting would be a hidden second-row write inside what is supposed to be one version's own transition; ACTIVE -> DEPRECATED is already a legal edge, so the caller demotes the old version first, as its own separate, auditable step. Read-then-write inside the transaction narrows the race the same way DS-LAKE-009-T03's versionNumber allocation does — same accepted-residual-window reasoning, not a new locking primitive, per smallest-safe-solution.

acceptance_criteria: Promotion updates metadata only — objectKey and checksum are byte-identical before and after.
Illegal transitions are refused.
The registry returns metadata only and never dataset rows.
Lineage resolves from any version back to its bronze artifact.
A dataset never has two ACTIVE versions.

verification.description: Record every artifact checksum before promotion and re-read after; assert equality. Also confirm the MinIO object count is unchanged.
verification.result: Structural proof + a real test, not a MinIO object-count measurement — NestJS holds no S3 credentials (decisions.storage) so an actual count comparison would need the same Python-write/TS-promote/Python-recheck split DS-LAKE-009B used, which this claim does not need: promoteVersionService never calls postToPython at all (asserted directly in the test via the shared `post` mock never firing) and never touches datasetArtifact. The one write (`datasetVersion.update({data: {status}}, select: {id, status}})`) is asserted call-for-call — no objectKey/checksum field appears in its `data` payload, so neither can change; since no MinIO call is made at all, the object count is provably unchanged by construction, not measured.

verification.description: Attempt ARCHIVED→ACTIVE and confirm refusal.
verification.result: Live test, not citation: 'DS-LAKE-010-V02: refuses ARCHIVED -> ACTIVE' asserts the exact pair the verification item names throws AppException, and that datasetVersion.update was never called. Backed by the pure predicate's own dedicated test ('refuses the exact backward pair DS-LAKE-010-V02 probes') at the unit level too — two layers, same claim.

verification.description: Inspect every registry response body and confirm no row payload leaks into it.
verification.result: Inspected every registry response body. listVersionsService: field-by-field map (id/datasetId/semanticVersion/artifactId/versionNumber/status/checksum/qualityScore/rowCount/columnCount/featureCount/missingPct/sizeBytes/durationMs/createdAt/createdBy) — no spread of the raw Prisma row, no field that could carry a data row. promoteVersionService: `{id, status}` only. getVersionLineageService: `{versionId, lineage}` where lineage is the frozen 4-field-per-artifact chain (id/type/checksum/objectKey) — no row values anywhere. Test asserts `res.data).not.toHaveProperty('rows')` on the lineage response directly.

features.result: Genuinely new implementation, unlike DS-LAKE-006/007/008 (all found pre-built) — confirmed by grep before starting: no promote/lineage/registry endpoint existed anywhere in the backend. Built: a pure, unit-tested state-machine predicate (lib/dataset-version-transitions.ts, 9 tests) enforcing the strict forward-only DRAFT->VALIDATED->ACTIVE->DEPRECATED->ARCHIVED chain; POST /:id/versions/:versionId/promote (metadata-only, AppException on illegal transitions, transactional single-ACTIVE-version guard); GET /:id/versions/:versionId/lineage (returns the frozen Save-time snapshot, not a live parentArtifactId walk — deliberately, since DS-LAKE-009B's cleanup can reclaim bytes a live walk would still point at); and one added field (checksum) closing listVersionsService's only registry-field gap. All 5 tasks and all 3 verification items verified with real tests (13 new service-level tests + 9 predicate tests = 22 new, all passing), zero new TypeScript errors (`tsc --noEmit`, confirmed via before/after file-set diff, matching this session's established discipline). Two real design decisions made and recorded rather than defaulted: same-state promote is idempotent-success not a 422, and single-ACTIVE-version conflicts are refused rather than auto-resolved by demoting the existing one.

features.title: Loader seam — enqueue, retry, pluggable sink
features.description: The asynchronous hand-off from a committed dataset to a serving layer. Scoped by user decision to the seam only: the job row, the enqueue point, the sink interface and independent retry. The TimescaleDB sink and the dashboard rewiring are deferred, because TimescaleDB does not exist in this repository and adding it is new infrastructure (CLAUDE.md §3).
features.scope_note: This feature ships a working loader with a no-op or logging sink. It is NOT marked completed on the strength of a stub: its acceptance criteria are about the seam's guarantees — enqueue, isolation from Save, retry — all of which are testable without a real sink.

tasks.title: LoaderJob model + status enum, mirroring the PreprocessingJob shape so the existing runner patterns transfer
tasks.result: LoaderJob model + LoaderJobStatus enum added to schema.prisma, mirroring PreprocessingJob's field names exactly (status/error/attempts/startedAt/finishedAt/createdBy/createdAt/updatedAt). datasetId/versionId are both REQUIRED (unlike PreprocessingJob's nullable draft/dataset pair) -- a loader has nothing to load until a DatasetVersion exists, so there is no draft-time case. Migration 20260813041139_ds_lake_011_loader_job applied; `pnpm db:generate` + `packages/prisma`'s own `pnpm build` (needed separately -- its dist/ types were stale after `prisma generate` alone) both run clean.

tasks.title: Sink interface with a single default implementation, so a Timescale sink can be added later without touching the enqueue path
tasks.result: LoaderSink interface (apps/backend/src/api/v1/loader/loader-sink.interface.ts): load(payload: {datasetId, versionId}) -- identifiers only, never a materialized frame (AC3). Single default implementation LogLoaderSink: logs the hand-off, deliberately not a silent no-op (a sink doing nothing observable would make LoaderJob.status a lie) and deliberately not a real serving-layer destination (no TimescaleDB in this repo, CLAUDE.md #3 -- see deferred[] below). Bound via a DI token (LOADER_SINK, loader.tokens.ts) in loader.module.ts -- swapping to a real sink later is a one-line change there, touching neither LoaderJobService nor its callers.

tasks.title: Enqueue after a successful Save, outside the save transaction
tasks.result: saveDraftAsDatasetService (dataset-draft.authorized.service.ts) calls `await this.loaderJobs.enqueue(dataset.id, version.id, user.id)` immediately AFTER its own $transaction block closes -- never inside it. Verified with a real test asserting call ORDER (transaction resolves, then enqueue fires), not just that both happen: 'DS-LAKE-011-T03: enqueues the loader job AFTER the transaction resolves, with the committed dataset/version ids'.

tasks.title: Independent retry with attempt counting, and boot-sweep semantics matching PreprocessingJobService
tasks.result: LoaderJobService (apps/backend/src/api/v1/loader/loader-job.service.ts) mirrors PreprocessingJobService's shape: onModuleInit sweeps every RUNNING row to FAILED on boot (single-replica assumption, same as the existing runner); retry() creates a NEW job row referencing the same dataset/version, carries `attempts` forward (incremented by the runner on start, not reset), leaves the original row's history untouched -- exact mirror of retryJobService's own pattern. No cancel surface built: nothing in this feature's AC/verification asks for one (smallest safe solution).

tasks.title: Job status endpoint so a future UI can report load progress
tasks.result: GET /:id/loader-jobs/:jobId (dataset-version.authorized.controller.ts) -> getLoaderJobStatusService, field-by-field response (id/datasetId/versionId/status/error/attempts/startedAt/finishedAt), no spread of the raw Prisma row. POST /:id/loader-jobs/:jobId/retry -> retryLoaderJobService, mirrors the existing job-retry endpoint's shape exactly.

acceptance_criteria: A loader failure never fails or rolls back Save.
A failed loader job can be retried independently and increments its attempt count.
The enqueue happens outside the save transaction.
No dataset row is read from the serving layer by any existing reader — MinIO remains the source of truth.
The deferred Timescale sink is recorded in deferred[], not silently implied as done.

verification.description: Force the sink to throw, save a dataset, and confirm the dataset and its version are committed while the LoaderJob lands FAILED.
verification.result: Live test (mocked Prisma, real LoaderJobService, real throwing sink), apps/backend/src/api/v1/loader/loader-job.service.spec.ts: 'DS-LAKE-011-V01: a throwing sink lands the job FAILED, with the error recorded' -- asserts the RUNNING transition happens, then the sink is called, then the row lands FAILED with the exact error message. A second test proves enqueue() itself never throws even when the sink fails -- the fire-and-forget boundary holds. The 'dataset and version are committed' half is proven separately in dataset-draft.authorized.service.spec.ts's own T03 test (enqueue only ever runs AFTER the transaction has already resolved) -- together the two tests cover exactly what V01 asks, at the two levels the seam actually spans.

verification.description: Retry the failed job and confirm a fresh attempt with attempts incremented, leaving the original row's history intact.
verification.result: Live test: 'DS-LAKE-011-V02: creates a NEW row referencing the same dataset/version, carrying attempts forward, leaving the original untouched' -- asserts retry() creates job-2 (not a mutation of job-1), attempts carried forward from the previous row (not reset to 0), and every subsequent Prisma update() call targets ONLY job-2's id -- job-1 (the original FAILED row) is never written to again, so its history survives exactly as it was.

verification.description: Kill the backend mid-load and confirm the boot sweep does not leave a job stuck RUNNING.
verification.result: Two halves. Boot-sweep half (the part this level of test CAN exercise without an actual process kill): 'sweeps every RUNNING row to FAILED on startup' -- asserts onModuleInit's updateMany call, mirroring PreprocessingJobService's own already-proven boot-sweep mechanism exactly (same query shape, same single-replica assumption already accepted for that runner). The 'kill the backend mid-load' framing is the SAME mechanism PreprocessingJobService already relies on and this session did not re-verify via an actual process kill -- reusing an already-proven pattern rather than re-proving it at the OS level for a second runner.

deferred.reason: TimescaleDB does not exist in this repository; adding it would be new infrastructure (CLAUDE.md §3). LoaderSink's single default implementation today is LogLoaderSink (logs the hand-off, does not persist to a serving layer).

deferred.item: Dashboard rewiring to read from the serving layer
deferred.reason: Depends on the TimescaleDB sink above landing first. AC3 (no dataset row is read from the serving layer by any existing reader — MinIO remains the source of truth) holds trivially today since no reader has been pointed at one.

features.result:
Genuinely new implementation, scoped by prior user decision (this feature's own scope_note) to the seam only. All 5 tasks and all 3 verification items completed with real test evidence: LoaderJob model + migration, LoaderSink interface + LogLoaderSink default implementation, enqueue wired into saveDraftAsDatasetService strictly after its transaction, LoaderJobService mirroring PreprocessingJobService's boot-sweep/retry shape, and 2 new endpoints (status/retry). 12 new tests across 3 files (7 in loader-job.service.spec.ts, 1 new + fixes in dataset-draft's spec, fixes in dataset-version's spec for the constructor signature change), all passing. tsc --noEmit and the full backend jest suite both confirmed against the SAME pre-existing baseline (8 failing suites in unrelated auth/plan/workspace/nodes areas, identical before and after via git stash comparison) -- zero regressions. AC4's deferred[] requirement satisfied explicitly above, not silently implied.

BUGFIX (found blocking real backend boot, DS-LAKE-005B-B-T01's E2E item, 2026-08-12; fixed 2026-08-13). `DatasetVersionModule` re-exported the bare `LoaderJobService` token -- `UnknownExportException` at every real `NestFactory.create`, invisible to Jest's isolated `TestingModule` specs (which never exercise this cross-module export path), so it shipped undetected. Root-caused by reading Nest's own `Module.validateExportedProvider` source directly (injector/module.js:302-317), not guessed: re-exporting a bare provider token only validates if that class is EITHER the current module's own `providers` entry (true for `PreprocessingJobService`, which is why ITS re-export never broke) OR one of the current module's imported MODULE classes themselves (`imports.includes(token)`, checked against module metatypes, not against what those modules export). `LoaderJobService` was neither -- it only exists via the imported `LoaderModule`, never listed as its own provider here. FIX: `exports: [PreprocessingJobService, LoaderModule]` -- re-export the whole owning module instead of cherry-picking its provider; `DatasetDraftModule` (the one real consumer) keeps the same transitive access. Verified LIVE, not by citation: `dotenvx run -- pnpm --filter backend dev` -- 'Nest application successfully started', 'Application running on port 4000'; `curl POST /api/v1/authorized/dataset-drafts` returns a real 401 from the auth guard, not a crash. Full backend suite (203 tests, same 8 pre-existing DI-error suites) and `tsc --noEmit` (same 4 pre-existing errors) both unchanged -- zero regressions from the fix itself.

features.title: Draft lifecycle auto-reclaim — scheduler, ACTIVE-branch eligibility, heartbeat
features.description: DS-LAKE-009B built the whole cleanup mechanism — eligibility predicate, lineage pinning, idempotent reclaim, objectReclaimedAt stamping, all live-verified — and then never wired anything to CALL it. This feature gives it a caller, and closes the ACTIVE-draft hole that makes a closed browser tab leak its artifacts forever. No new eligibility logic beyond the ACTIVE branch; no new reclaim path.
userDecisions: SCHEDULER MECHANISM (resolved): option C — `setInterval(...).unref()` in `onModuleInit`, NOT `@nestjs/schedule`. Rejected A (new dependency for one interval, CLAUDE.md §3) and B (external cron: token management, invisible to the repo, launchd on macOS). This codebase already uses exactly this pattern for the same class of work — `PreprocessingJobService.scheduleStragglerSweep` — so C reuses an established precedent instead of introducing a second scheduling idiom.

ACTIVE-DRAFT WINDOW (resolved): TIERED, not a single 10-minute rule. The user asked for 10 minutes; taken as the right answer for the case they were describing (a draft abandoned before anything was fetched) and NOT generalised to every ACTIVE draft, because a 10-minute blanket rule would destroy a real BRONZE that cost minutes of PI fetch while the engineer was in a meeting.

HEARTBEAT (resolved, this session): the ledger's open decision assumed a draft PATCH route to ride on; none exists (23 routes on authorized/dataset-drafts, zero @Patch/@Put). New POST :id/touch route instead, ownership-checked via the existing assertDraftAccess, guarded to status:'ACTIVE' so it is a no-op on a SAVED/ABANDONED draft. Client beats every 60s, gated on document.visibilityState === 'visible', so a backgrounded or closed tab stops beating and idle detection measures real absence, not silence.

EMPTY-DRAFT RECLAIM (resolved, this session): selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts is artifact-keyed, so an ACTIVE draft owning zero artifacts produces zero candidate rows and can never surface there — and there is nothing to reclaim in MinIO for it anyway. 'Reclaimed' for this case is therefore a DRAFT-LEVEL status transition to ABANDONED (no row deleted, no object touched, per decisions.cleanup_scope), run as a second pass in the same sweep tick, gated on CLEANUP_ACTIVE_EMPTY_MINUTES and 'artifacts: { none: { objectReclaimedAt: null } }'. This reverses env.config.ts's prior note that no inactivity-based auto-abandon path exists — that note is updated, not contradicted.

WINDOW VALUES (confirmed, this session): CLEANUP_ACTIVE_EMPTY_MINUTES=15, CLEANUP_ACTIVE_IDLE_HOURS=6, CLEANUP_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS=300000 (<=0 disables the sweep). 15 minutes gives a 60s heartbeat 15 missed beats of slack before a visibly-open tab is misjudged as gone.

CORRECTION to this feature's own SCHEDULER MECHANISM entry: it claims 'this codebase already uses exactly this pattern for the same class of work — PreprocessingJobService.scheduleStragglerSweep'. Verified false on direct read: scheduleStragglerSweep is a one-shot setTimeout(...).unref(), fired once per cancelled job, not a recurring setInterval, and its interval is a hardcoded module constant with no env var. There is no setInterval anywhere in the backend today and @nestjs/schedule is not a dependency — this feature adds the FIRST setInterval in the backend. Option C (setInterval(...).unref() in onModuleInit) is still correct, but on its own merits (smallest change, reuses the .unref()/swallow-errors idiom that setTimeout call and the three existing onModuleInit boot sweeps establish), not on a precedent that doesn't exist.

tasks.title: Tiered ACTIVE-draft eligibility: artifact-less drafts on a short window, artifact-bearing drafts on a long one
tasks.scope_note: TWO new env windows beside the existing two, not a reuse: CLEANUP_ACTIVE_EMPTY_MINUTES (15) is NOT part of the eligibility predicate -- it cannot be, because selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts/reportCleanupEligibility is artifact-keyed and a draft with ZERO artifacts produces zero candidate rows, so it can never be visited there. It is a separate DRAFT-LEVEL pass (ArtifactCleanupAdminService.autoAbandonEmptyActiveDrafts) run once per sweep, querying DatasetDraft directly (status ACTIVE, updatedAt past the window, zero live artifacts) and transitioning matching rows to ABANDONED -- no MinIO object involved, nothing was ever fetched. CLEANUP_ACTIVE_IDLE_HOURS (6) IS part of the predicate (CleanupEligibilityConfig.activeIdleHours, artifact-cleanup-eligibility.ts) and applies when the draft DOES own a live artifact -- a real PI fetch cost minutes, and an engineer may return to it. Both measure from draft.updatedAt, matching the SAVED/ABANDONED branches' own established convention (and the bug DS-LAKE-009B-T08 already fixed once by moving OFF artifact.createdAt). An ACTIVE draft is never lineage-pinned -- no DatasetVersion can reference it yet -- so the pin check is a no-op on the idle-tier branch and must not be assumed to protect anything there.
tasks.result: CleanupEligibilityConfig.activeIdleHours (artifact-cleanup-eligibility.ts) drives the artifact-bearing ACTIVE tier inside reportCleanupEligibility/selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts. The artifact-less tier is a separate draft-level pass, ArtifactCleanupAdminService.autoAbandonEmptyActiveDrafts -- see that task's own scope_note, corrected this session to stop describing CLEANUP_ACTIVE_EMPTY_MINUTES as part of the predicate. LIVE-VERIFIED against real Postgres + real MinIO + real Python in one run() call: an idle-tier-survivor draft (artifact-bearing, 30min old, inside 6h) stayed ACTIVE with objectReclaimedAt still null; an idle-tier-reclaim draft (artifact-bearing, 7h old) had its real 2431-byte MinIO object actually deleted (Python confirmed deletedObjects:1) and objectReclaimedAt stamped. Both outcomes in the SAME sweep pass, proving the tier discriminates rather than blanket-reclaiming (V02). EMERGENT BEHAVIOUR observed live and judged benign, not a bug: in the V02 pass, the artifact-bearing idle-tier-reclaim draft flipped ACTIVE -> ABANDONED in the SAME run() call that reclaimed its only artifact -- the artifact pass stamped objectReclaimedAt first, which made the draft satisfy autoAbandonEmptyActiveDrafts' `artifacts: {none: {objectReclaimedAt: null}}` filter on the SAME tick (its updatedAt, 7h old, already cleared the much shorter 15-minute empty-draft cutoff too). No acceptance criterion is violated -- AC2 only protects the SHORT window, and this reclaim happened on the long idle window -- but it means a draft can go ACTIVE -> ABANDONED as a second-order consequence of the artifact pass within one tick, not just via its own direct empty-draft check. See autoAbandonEmptyActiveDrafts' updated doc comment.

tasks.title: Periodic sweep caller: setInterval in ArtifactCleanupAdminService.onModuleInit
tasks.scope_note: CLEANUP_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS (proposed 300_000), with `<= 0` disabling the sweep entirely — needed for tests and for an operator who wants the admin endpoint to stay the only trigger. `.unref()` so the timer never holds the process open at shutdown, matching scheduleStragglerSweep. Errors are logged and swallowed: a failed sweep must never crash the app, and every artifact it would have reclaimed stays eligible for the next tick. NO LOCK: overlap across replicas is safe by construction, not by luck — DS-LAKE-009B-T06 already proved candidates are queried WHERE objectReclaimedAt IS NULL and delete_prefix on an absent prefix returns 0 rather than erroring. VERIFY FIRST: confirm ArtifactCleanupModule is actually imported by AppModule; if it is not, onModuleInit never fires and the whole task is dead on arrival.
tasks.result: ArtifactCleanupAdminService now implements OnModuleInit/OnApplicationShutdown. onModuleInit starts setInterval(() => void this.sweep(), env.CLEANUP_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS).unref() when the value is > 0 (default 300_000ms); <= 0 skips scheduling entirely, verified live: called onModuleInit() directly with CLEANUP_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS=3000 against real Postgres/MinIO/Python (no HTTP call anywhere in the calling script) and observed a real 'trigger=interval' sweep log line ~3s later, unattended. sweep() wraps run({dryRun:false, trigger:'interval'}) in try/catch, logging and swallowing -- confirmed live and via a unit test that a throwing run() does not crash the process and the NEXT tick still completes successfully (not merely that the timer stays registered). ArtifactCleanupModule WAS already imported by AppModule (app.module.ts:24,66) -- T03's own 'verify first' instruction confirmed the task was not dead on arrival. No lock: verified both in a unit test (overlapping run() calls) and live (two back-to-back real run() calls, V05) that re-selection is impossible once objectReclaimedAt is stamped. LIVE-VERIFIED the 'admin endpoint unchanged' half specifically (previously only unit-covered that no timer schedules at <=0): constructed a standalone instance with CLEANUP_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS=0, confirmed onModuleInit() logs 'sweep disabled' and starts no timer, then called run({dryRun:true}) -- the exact call runCleanupController makes -- against real Postgres and confirmed a normal result (scanned:64, a real trigger=admin log line). The admin controller has zero code-level coupling to the scheduler (grep confirms runCleanupController never references sweepTimer/onModuleInit), so this is a structural guarantee (DS-LAKE-009B-T07's own precedent style) now also demonstrated live.

tasks.title: Draft-level reclaim reporting so a growing bucket is diagnosable rather than inferred
tasks.scope_note: The sweep's own log line should state, per run: candidates examined, reclaimed count, bytes reclaimed, and the count skipped per REASON (lineage-pinned / inside window / active job). Without the per-reason breakdown a sweep that reclaims nothing is indistinguishable from a sweep that found nothing — which is exactly the ambiguity that let both gaps in this feature's finding sit undetected.
tasks.result: Additive reportCleanupEligibility (artifact-cleanup-eligibility.ts) returns {eligible, skipped: {lineage_pinned, shared_final_object, no_draft, inside_window}} alongside the unchanged selectCleanupEligibleArtifacts delegate, so DS-LAKE-009B-T08's original tests needed zero modification. ArtifactCleanupAdminService adds the one skip reason it alone can compute (active_job, a live PreprocessingJob reference) and a bytesReclaimed running total (BigInt, summed only after Python confirms deletion, converted to a JSON-safe string). Every run logs one summary line unconditionally: 'Cleanup sweep (trigger=X, dryRun=Y): examined N, reclaimed R (B bytes), failed F, skipped {...}, auto-abandoned D empty draft(s).' The invariant examined == reclaimed + failed + sum(skipped) is asserted in a dedicated unit test and held on real production-shaped data in the live pass (66 = 1 + 0 + 65; second run 65 = 0 + 0 + 65). The bytesReclaimed path itself was the session's own near-miss: a live probe against real Postgres confirmed Prisma + @prisma/adapter-pg returns DatasetArtifact.sizeBytes as a genuine bigint (not a string/number some driver adapters return for int8), so `bytesReclaimed += sizeBytes` cannot silently throw and get swallowed by sweep()'s catch -- a unit test with two real bigint sizes (205_760n + 1_024n) locks the accumulation path in, and the live V02 pass confirmed a non-zero '2431 bytes' in a real log line, not the '(0 bytes)' every prior test fixture would have hidden.

acceptance_criteria: An ACTIVE draft with no artifacts becomes eligible after the short window and is reclaimed by the periodic sweep with no operator action.
An ACTIVE draft that owns a BRONZE artifact is NOT reclaimed on the short window.
A wizard left open on Step 3.1 without edits does not become eligible.
The sweep runs without any HTTP call, and disabling it via env leaves the admin endpoint working unchanged.
A sweep failure does not crash the process and does not prevent the next tick.
No SAVED-draft or ABANDONED-draft behaviour changes, and no FINAL artifact becomes eligible.
Every sweep logs reclaimed count, bytes, and skips broken down by reason.

verification.description: Seed a real ACTIVE draft with zero artifacts and updatedAt past the short window; run the real sweep against real Postgres and MinIO; confirm reclaimed and stamped.
verification.result: FULL LIVE PASS, real Postgres + real MinIO + real Python (uvicorn :8000), dryRun:false, run() called directly (DS-LAKE-009B's own established verification pattern). Seeded a real ACTIVE draft, zero artifacts, updatedAt backdated 20 minutes (past the 15-minute default CLEANUP_ACTIVE_EMPTY_MINUTES). The SAME run() call that performed V02's reclaim flipped this draft to ABANDONED via the autoAbandonEmptyActiveDrafts pass -- no operator action, no HTTP call. Probe row deleted afterward; zero residue confirmed by re-inventory.

verification.description: PROVE THE TIER BITES BOTH WAYS: an ACTIVE draft WITH a real artifact, updatedAt past the SHORT window but inside the long one, must survive the same sweep run that reclaims V01's draft. One run, two drafts, opposite outcomes — a test that only proves reclamation cannot distinguish a working tier from a blanket rule.
verification.result: PROVED THE TIER BITES BOTH WAYS in ONE run() call, per the verification item's own standard: seeded (a) an ACTIVE draft owning a real 2431-byte MinIO object, updatedAt 30 minutes old -- past the 15-minute empty tier but inside the 6-hour idle tier -- and (b) an ACTIVE draft owning a real 2431-byte MinIO object, updatedAt 7 hours old -- past the idle tier. The single run() call left (a) untouched (status ACTIVE, objectReclaimedAt null) while genuinely reclaiming (b): Python confirmed deletedObjects:1 and objectReclaimedAt was stamped with a real timestamp. features.title: Raw validation holdout — validate_data.parquet split at BRONZE, replayed for post-training validation
features.progress_note: All 5 tasks and all 5 verification items completed (2026-08-19). T01-T04 built the holdout selection/split/persistence/replay mechanism; T05 wired it into a real training run (claim()/complete(), train.pys holdout-scoring block), finding and fixing two real bugs along the way (a response-model field silently stripped since T03; a feature_spec.json reshape collision on kind). V02/V03/V04 were proven in T05s own pass; V01 (holdout absence traced live through BRONZE/SILVER/GOLD, with FINAL confirmed structurally via a fresh code read) and V05 (a real scikit-learn model trained and scored on both a real test split and a real replayed holdout, using train.pys own functions directly) were proven live in a follow-up pass after being left honestly pending. Not covered anywhere this session: an actual Docker training-container spawn end to end (trainning-container.authorized.service.ts) -- the orchestration boundary is unit-tested (claim() exact call args) and the training/scoring mechanism itself is live-proven (this V05 pass), but the two have not been exercised together through a real container. T06 (added later): the holdout picker moved from Step 2 to Step 3.1 (EDA) -- see that task's own result for the reversal of userDecisions[0]'s original 'picked at Step 2' framing and the new server-side re-split endpoint this required.
features.description: A held-out slice of RAW rows, split at BRONZE and stored as a sidecar, used to validate a trained model against data that never touched the cleaning or feature pipeline. USER DECISION: split at BRONZE, not FINAL — the point is to ask 'does this model work on data as it actually arrives', which is a stronger and different question than a test-set score.
userDecisions: HOLDOUT WINDOW AND LEAD-IN (resolved): the user picks the holdout as a DATE RANGE at Step 2, beside the existing fetch range — not a row count, not a percentage. Lead-in is NOT a user choice: it is inferred, because the rows before the holdout boundary are already inside the fetch window and cost nothing extra to carry. Lead-in is configured as a DURATION (`HOLDOUT_LEAD_IN_DURATION`, default 7d), never a row count: `rolling(60)` spans one hour at a 1-minute interval and 60 hours at a 1-hour one, so a fixed row count means something different for every interval while a duration means the same thing. The interval is already known at materialize time (Step 2 sets it), so the duration converts to rows there.

REVERSED BY DS-LAKE-018-T06 (explicit user request, later session): the SELECTION POINT moved from Step 2 to Step 3.1 (EDA) — the user now sees their fetched data (Step 3.1's charts) before picking a holdout, rather than choosing a validation window against a time range they only knew abstractly. Everything else this decision states (date range not a row count/percentage, lead-in inferred as a duration, resolved at materialize time) is UNCHANGED — only WHEN the user is asked moved, not HOW the holdout itself is expressed or computed. See T06's own result for why this forced a new server-side re-split endpoint (the artifact is already materialized, with no holdout, by the time Step 3.1 mounts).
SPLIT STAGE (resolved): BRONZE. The holdout is raw so it can validate the model the way production will feed it.

STORAGE (resolved): a separate `validate_data.parquet` sidecar, not a `__split` column and not a stored range. Leakage becomes STRUCTURAL rather than conventional — every code path that reads the artifact would see a marker column and would have to remember to filter it. That is the same argument `BoundedSample`'s brand exists for ('convention alone already failed once'). `presign_artifact` already takes `sidecars: list[str]` and returns null for an absent one, so the transport needs no change at all.

SUPERSEDED BY DS-LAKE-023 (2026-08-25), for NEW datasets only — this feature's own completion (100%, V01/V05 proven live) is unaffected and describes what it tested, which remains true. What moved: the split point (T01/T03 here cut at BRONZE before features; DS-LAKE-023-T01 cuts after features, in the reordered create-mode wizard only). What stays LIVE, legacy-path only, for every holdout picked before DS-LAKE-023 or picked in edit mode (features locked there, so it never opts into the reorder): HOLDOUT_LEAD_IN, max_replay_lookback's compound-lookback walk, replay_holdout / replay_holdout_for_run and their lead-in refusal, resplit_holdout (mechanism unchanged; 'pristine' now means pristine BRONZE specifically, since DS-LAKE-023's reordered path re-derives its own SILVER from that same BRONZE instead of resplitting anything). scalingParams (T02 here) is UNCHANGED and now the ONLY remaining transform-transfer mechanism on both paths — DS-LAKE-023-T03's prepare-holdout-for-run consumes the exact same field. The resolved no-imputation decision (openDecisions[0]/T04's own scope_note) is UNCHANGED and answers DS-LAKE-023's own cleaning question too: a feature-bearing holdout is never cleaned either.
findings: SPLITTING AT BRONZE DOES NOT MEAN THE HOLDOUT SKIPS THE PIPELINE. A raw holdout has none of the derived columns feature engineering creates, so `model.predict(test[feature_cols])` fails on a column mismatch. What the holdout must skip is TRAINING, not TRANSFORMING — the replay in T04 is deliberately the same work production must do on every incoming batch, which makes this an end-to-end pipeline validation rather than a model-only one. That is a feature of the choice, not a workaround for it.

BLOCKER — FITTED SCALER PARAMETERS ARE NOT PERSISTED ANYWHERE. `feature_spec.json` records `scaling: [{tag, method}]` — WHICH method, never the mean/std/min/max that method fit on the train rows. `to_model_ready` fits and transforms in one pass and discards the parameters. Scaling the holdout against its OWN statistics is a DIFFERENT transform from the one the model learned, and it fails silently: predictions come out plausible and wrong, not erroneous. Nothing downstream can catch that. T02 is a hard prerequisite for T04.

LAG AND ROLLING FEATURES NEED LEAD-IN ROWS. `lag` and `rolling` read rows BEFORE the row being computed, so a contiguous holdout window cannot compute them for its own first rows. `validate_data.parquet` must carry lead-in rows ahead of the holdout boundary, trimmed after replay. NOTE: DS-LAKE-005B-B-T01's grep result concluded `BoundedSample` needs no lookback margin because feature engineering was leaving the client entirely — that conclusion was correct for its own scope and does NOT cover this case. Recorded as a genuine exception, not a contradiction.

HOLDOUT ROWS MUST BE CUT FROM data.parquet TOO. Writing a sidecar does not remove them from the main file; they would flow BRONZE -> SILVER -> GOLD -> FINAL and land in the training set exactly as before. This is the single easiest thing in the feature to get wrong and the hardest to notice, because every number still looks reasonable.
openDecisions: RESOLVED (user decision, 2026-08-19, asked directly before implementing T04): DOES REPLAY INCLUDE IMPUTATION? — NO. The holdout stays fully raw: apply_features -> select_columns -> to_model_ready only, no fill/imputation step. A raw holdout carries Bad cells and gaps that feed through untouched; the holdout score is deliberately pessimistic where that happens rather than matching production's own imputation, and is not directly comparable to the test-set score for that reason. Implemented exactly this way in T04 — no apply_operations call exists in replay_holdout at all.

LEAD-IN ROW COUNT. Derivable as the max lag/window across the recipe, but whether it is computed at split time (needs the Step 4 recipe, which does not exist yet at BRONZE) or over-provisioned to a fixed margin is a real design fork with a real cost either way.

column_stats.json SCOPE. Computed over train rows only, or all rows? Over all rows, the statistics the engineer reads include data the model never saw. Over train only, the sidecar stops describing the file it sits beside. Both are defensible; neither is chosen.

tasks.title: Holdout date-range selection at Step 2, with lead-in inferred from a configured duration
tasks.scope_note:
Reuse `CropTimeInputs`/`DateTimePicker` (data-cropping-chart.tsx) rather than a new picker. FOUR guards, each catching a failure that would otherwise surface far from its cause:

(1) HOLDOUT INSIDE THE FETCH WINDOW — refuse at selection time, not after a multi-minute fetch discovers there are no rows there.

(2) TRAIN REMAINDER SUFFICIENT — `train.py` refuses below 30 LABELLED rows after its own 80/20 split, and a lab target on a 1-minute grid has orders of magnitude fewer labels than rows. Warn while the window is being chosen, when it is still cheap to change.

(3) LEAD-IN ACTUALLY AVAILABLE — if `holdout.from - leadIn` precedes `fetch.from`, the lead-in is short. State how much was actually captured rather than silently writing less than configured; T04's own check is the backstop, but discovering it there means discovering it after training.

(4) TRAILING IS RECOMMENDED, NOT REQUIRED — a mid-window holdout leaves the training set in two pieces, and lag/rolling features computed ACROSS that gap read rows from the wrong side of it. Warn, do not block: holding out a specific upset period is a legitimate reason to accept that.

Record the resolved lead-in row count in the sidecar or the artifact row, so T04 can check it without re-deriving the duration against an interval it would have to look up.
corrections: openDecisions[0] ('does replay include imputation?') is marked NOT DECIDED, but T04's own scope_note asserts 'the resolved no-imputation decision' as settled fact — those two statements inside the same feature contradict each other. openDecisions[1] (lead-in row count: derived from the not-yet-existing Step 4 recipe vs. over-provisioned to a fixed margin) reads as already answered by userDecisions[0], which chose a configured DURATION with a default (7d) — over-provisioned, not derived. tasks.title: PREREQUISITE: persist fitted scaler parameters in feature_spec.json
tasks.scope_note: `to_model_ready` must return what it fit; `build_feature_spec` records it as `scalingParams`. Deliberately NOT part of `featureHash` — the hash answers 'was this the same recipe', and the same recipe over the same rows always fits the same parameters, so including them adds nothing and would churn the hash for a non-change. Ship this with a test that a holdout scaled with recorded parameters differs from one scaled against its own statistics; without that assertion the field could be written and never actually used.
tasks.result: `_scale_column(values, method, params=None)` (feature_service.py) now returns `(scaled_array, params_used)` instead of a bare array — fits `params` when None (today's behaviour), or applies SUPPLIED params without re-fitting when given (the primitive DS-LAKE-018-T04's holdout replay needs). tasks.title: Replay endpoint: raw holdout -> model-ready frame, with a hard lead-in sufficiency check
tasks.scope_note:
Runs apply_features -> select_columns -> to_model_ready with scaler parameters SUPPLIED, never re-fit. NO apply_operations — the resolved no-imputation decision means the holdout stays raw; only feature/select/scale run.

LEAD-IN CHECK IS A REFUSAL, NOT A WARNING: compute the recipe's true maximum lookback from feature_spec.json (a lag on a rolling column compounds — lag(5) of rolling(60) needs 65) and REFUSE when the captured lead-in is short, naming both numbers and the shortfall. The alternative is the silent failure this check exists to prevent: the holdout's first rows get null or wrong lag values, feed straight into predict(), and depress the metric with no trace of why. Trim lead-in rows after replay, before returning — they are scaffolding for the feature computation, not rows to score.

tasks.title: Move holdout selection from Step 2 to Step 3.1 (EDA), so the user sees their data before picking a holdout
tasks.scope_note: Explicit user request, reversing userDecisions[0]'s original 'picked at Step 2' framing (see that entry's own reversal note). NOT a UI-only move: `_split_holdout` runs once, at materialize time, and `useDatasetBronzeWarm` fires that materialize the moment Step 2's fetch completes — BEFORE Step 3.1 mounts, and `ensureBronzeArtifactId` never re-materializes once an artifact exists (`if (artifactId) return artifactId`). A holdout picked at Step 3.1 therefore cannot reach the server through the existing materialize path at all; it needs a new way to reach BRONZE after the fact.
tasks.result:
APPROACH: a new endpoint re-splits an EXISTING, PRISTINE (never-split) BRONZE against a holdout, without re-fetching from the source, always writing a NEW artifact (artifacts are immutable by convention) rather than mutating in place. The source is ALWAYS the draft's pristine root, never the previous split result — `_split_holdout` is lossy (once a holdout is applied, `data.parquet` no longer contains those rows), and reconstructing the original frame from `validate_data.parquet` is not reliably possible: it would need the PREVIOUS holdout boundary to partition the lead-in overlap out, and that boundary is not persisted anywhere reachable (`build_manifest` never included `validation_holdout_from`, and NestJS never wrote `DatasetArtifact.validationHoldoutFrom` on the materialize path either — a pre-existing gap, found and fixed for this new endpoint only, not backfilled onto materialize). Splitting fresh from pristine every time is idempotent and needs no reconstruction.

PYTHON: new `artifact_service.resplit_holdout()` (services/artifact_service.py), reusing `_split_holdout` VERBATIM (same function T03 wrote) plus the same two post-split guards `materialize()` applies (`assert_frame_is_usable`, the 0-row validate refusal). New `ResplitHoldoutRequest` schema (`holdout` REQUIRED, not optional — clearing a holdout never reaches Python at all, see NESTJS below). New `POST /v1/preprocess/resplit-holdout` router endpoint, same `_run`/`ArtifactStatsResponse` pattern as its neighbours. `ArtifactStatsSchema` (backend) gained `validation_holdout_from` — previously silently dropped at that exact parse boundary; added here because the new endpoint needs to persist it for `replay_holdout_for_run` to work on a re-split artifact, not as a general fix of the pre-existing materialize-path gap.

NESTJS: new `resplitDraftHoldoutService` — resolves the draft's PRISTINE root by walking UP from `currentArtifactId`'s own `parentArtifactId` chain (not a direct `{type: 'BRONZE', parentArtifactId: null}` query — a draft can carry more than one BRONZE root across separate wizard runs, each re-fetch minting a new `runId` chain, and only the chain the draft is CURRENTLY on is correct). REFUSES (422) if that root's `validationRowCount` is already set — it was split at materialize time (a legacy dataset, or one created before this task), so re-splitting it would permanently shed rows; the fix there is re-fetching, not re-splitting. `holdout: null` clears the holdout WITHOUT calling Python at all — the pristine root already IS the no-holdout artifact, so this is a pointer move (`datasetDraft.currentArtifactId` back to the root). A real split writes a new BRONZE with `parentArtifactId` set to the pristine root and moves the pointer to it, inside a `$transaction`. New `POST /:id/holdout` controller endpoint + `ResplitDraftHoldoutDto`. Checked, not assumed: `lib/artifact-cleanup-eligibility.ts` never reads `parentArtifactId` — a superseded split-BRONZE releases by age on the normal ACTIVE/SAVED branch like any other intermediate, so repeated holdout edits do not leak artifacts.

CLIENT: `ValidationHoldoutSection` extracted from step-2-raw-data.tsx into `processing/validation-holdout-section.tsx`, behaviour otherwise unchanged. Now derives its fetch/raw window from `dwRawDatasetAtom`'s own first/last row timestamps (not `dwCustomDateRangeAtom`, which can be null — a preset-period fetch never writes it, and is always null-safe-guarded against by Step 2's own effect timing that no longer applies once this section lives at Step 3.1) and its interval from the same `dwFetchConfigAtom`/`dwCustomIntervalAtom`/`dwTimeRangeAtom` atoms Step 2 used locally. Holdout validates against this raw/fetch window, never the crop range — crop is a downstream preprocessing operation on a DIFFERENT frame than the BRONZE-level split. New `useDatasetHoldoutResplit` hook calls the service and points `dwDraftArtifactIdAtom` at whatever artifact the server returns — sufficient on its own to refresh Step 3.1's whole card, since `useDatasetFeaturePreviewSample` keys its fetch effect on that atom and `DataAnalysisCard`'s server-backed tabs read it directly. Fires ONLY from the section's own `commit`/`handleToggle` (an actual user action) — its atom-resync effect (hydration, wizard reset) never calls it, so edit-mode hydration and step-navigation cannot trigger a spurious re-split. Lifted into `Step31EDA` (not owned inside the section) because Next must stay disabled while a re-split is in flight, same reasoning as gating Next on the existing readiness-phase `isBusy` — advancing mid-split would move Step 3.2 onto an artifact about to be replaced.

TESTS: python — 5 new tests in `test_artifact_service_resplit_holdout.py` (split content matches `_split_holdout`'s own proven shape; train+validate UNION reconstructs every original row; re-splitting the SAME pristine source twice with different windows each independently reconstructs the full row set — the regression that matters, proving no cumulative shedding; the 0-row-match and whole-window refusals). Full python suite: 668 passed, 66 skipped, one pre-existing unrelated failure confirmed via `git stash` (same `column_stats_key` gap T02/T03/T04/T05 already recorded). NestJS — 6 new tests in `dataset-draft.authorized.service.spec.ts` (draft-not-found and no-artifact-yet guards; walks a non-root artifact up to its BRONZE root and reads FROM the root, not the current artifact; refuses 422 on an already-split root; `holdout: null` moves the pointer without calling Python; a real split writes `parentArtifactId`/`validationHoldoutFrom` correctly and moves `currentArtifactId`). Backend `tsc --noEmit` and full `jest` run: clean/passing except pre-existing unrelated failures confirmed via `git stash` (auth-module DI errors, unrelated controller-spec DI stubs — none touch dataset-draft/dataset-version). Client `tsc --noEmit` and `vitest`: clean/passing except pre-existing unrelated failures confirmed via `git stash` (feature-preset.test.ts, plants/canvas/settings suites, step-5-review-save.test.tsx — none reference step-2-raw-data.tsx, step-3-1-EDA.tsx, validation-holdout-section.tsx, or use-dataset-holdout-resplit.ts).

acceptance_criteria: A dataset with a holdout selection produces validate_data.parquet beside its BRONZE artifact.
The holdout rows are ABSENT from data.parquet and therefore from every downstream stage and from training.
feature_spec.json records the scaler parameters fitted on the train rows.
The replayed holdout has exactly the same columns, in the same order, as the frame the model was trained on.
The holdout is scaled with the train's fitted parameters, never re-fit on itself.
Lag and rolling features are correct for the holdout's first rows, not null or wrong.
Holdout metrics are reported separately from test metrics, and the two are comparable at a glance.
A dataset with no holdout selection behaves exactly as today.
rowCount keeps its existing meaning; the holdout count is a separate field.
The holdout can be picked (or changed) at Step 3.1, after the user has seen their fetched data, and reaches the server as a re-split of the existing artifact — not silently discarded.

features.title: Split the Step 5 validation gate into blocking and advisory checks
features.description: Validation is currently all-or-nothing: any failed check sets status FAILED and Save is refused in three places. In practice the checks are not equally serious — a duplicate timestamp or a broken frame shape means the artifact is unusable, while zero-variance tags and a high outlier fraction mean the DATA is worth questioning, which is a judgment the engineer should make rather than have made for them. Split the checks by severity so the first class blocks and the second warns prominently.
userDecisions: BLOCKING SET (resolved): schema, duplicate_timestamps, and feature_consistency-when-failed. Advisory: missing_values, statistical, completeness — surfaced prominently, never blocking. missing_values was confirmed as advisory explicitly rather than assumed from 'the rest': a 20% missing rate is a bigger finding than an outlier fraction, so it was put back to the user separately and confirmed.

FEATURE_CONSISTENCY SPLITS ON skipped, NOT ON passed (resolved in two steps, both confirmed): a SKIP passes — a missing feature_spec is the normal state of a dataset that skipped Step 4, and `promoteDraftArtifactToFinalService`'s own doc comment plus DS-LAKE-012-V03's live 3-stage chain both establish such a dataset must stay saveable; blocking the skip would make every no-feature-engineering dataset permanently unsaveable. A FAIL blocks — a spec that EXISTS and whose columns do not match the artifact is a real inconsistency, and training against it means predicting from columns the model was never fitted on. The predicate is therefore `passed === false && skipped === false`, not `!passed`.
findings: THE GATE IS ENFORCED IN THREE PLACES, NOT ONE, AND TWO OF THEM ARE SERVER-SIDE ON PURPOSE. `promoteDraftArtifactToFinalService` refuses 422 unless it re-validates PASS; `saveDraftAsDatasetService` re-validates AGAIN and refuses 422; `step-5-review-save.tsx` disables Save via `validationBlocking`. DS-LAKE-009-T04's own reasoning for the server checks is 'never trusting a client-supplied report' — relaxing only the UI would produce a clickable Save that then 422s, which is worse than a disabled one.

THE CLEANEST SEAM IS `status` ITSELF, WHICH LEAVES ALL THREE GATES UNTOUCHED. If `run_validation` computes `status` from BLOCKING failures only and reports advisory failures in a separate field, every existing gate keeps working with zero edits — they all read `status`. `quality_score` also needs no change: the user's own sample already reads 90.0 with a single advisory failure, so the graded number was already doing the right thing while the binary status overrode it.

THE ADVISORY IN THE SAMPLE IS A REAL FINDING, NOT NOISE — which is exactly why it must stay visible. 9 zero-variance tags and 2 tags at an 18.1% outlier fraction will produce a model whose metrics look fine and whose behaviour does not. Downgrading the check from blocking to advisory is only defensible if the warning is prominent AND persisted, so that whoever reads a model's results later can still see what the dataset was flagged for.

tasks.title: Severity classification in validation_service.py, with status derived from blocking failures only
tasks.scope_note: Add a severity per check (blocking | advisory) as a real field on the response, not a client-side lookup table — a client list would drift from the server's own weighting the first time a check is added. `status` becomes PASS when no BLOCKING check failed, regardless of advisories; a new `advisory_failures` list carries the rest, alongside the existing `failed_checks` which keeps its current meaning (every failure, either class) so nothing reading it today changes meaning. CHECK_WEIGHTS and compute_quality_score are NOT touched: the score is a graded summary and an advisory failure genuinely should cost points — that is what makes 90.0 informative rather than decorative.

features.title: Preset range cutoff — per-tag Range from the Excel/CSV feature preset drives Step 3.2 outlier cutoff
features.description: Each Excel sheet carries several numbered configs (config_no), each with its own features[] and its own per-feature `range` string. That range is currently imported into the preset JSON and then dropped — nothing downstream reads it. Surface it in Step 3.2's CutOffSection as a per-tag cutoff proposal, sourced from the preset rather than hand-typed, with provenance back to the config it came from.
findings: RANGE IS FREE TEXT, NOT A NUMBER PAIR, and one real preset already exercises five distinct shapes: `"-"` (no range, 2 features), `"105-120 C"` / `"132-140 C"` / `"138-150 C"` / `"145-157 C"` / `"155-165 C"` (closed, integer, unit C), `">21500 kg/hr"` x5 and `">13000 kg/hr"` (lower-open), `"230-300 tph"` (closed, different unit), `"2.5-10 cP"` (decimal min), `"0.85-1.2"` (decimal both, NO unit). Any parser must be written against this observed grammar, not an assumed one.

THE HYPHEN IS BOTH SEPARATOR AND MINUS SIGN. No negative bound appears in s-204-no1, but a delta feature or a sub-zero temperature will produce `"-5-10"`, which a naive split on '-' resolves to garbage silently rather than raising. This must be handled explicitly and tested, because the failure mode is a wrong cutoff, not an exception.

THE RANGE UNIT IS NOT GUARANTEED TO MATCH THE TAG'S OWN ENGINEERING UNIT, and this preset proves units already mix WITHIN one config: FIC114A-D/I.PV are quoted in kg/hr while FIC204.PV is quoted in tph, and the Reflux_ratio formula itself divides the kg/hr group by 1000 before adding it to FY107.CPV. A cutoff applied without reconciling units is wrong by 1000x and every resulting value still looks plausible — the same silent-wrongness class as DS-LAKE-018's unpersisted scaler parameters.

AN `equation` FEATURE'S RANGE CANNOT BE APPLIED AT STEP 3.2 AT ALL. The derived column does not exist until Step 4 (feature_service.py). In s-204-no1: 12 of 15 features are `raw_tag` with a usable range, 1 is an equation with a real range (`Reflux_ratio... = 0.85-1.2`), and 2 are equations with `range: "-"`. So the Step 3.2 surface can only ever serve the raw_tag subset — see openDecisions.

`">21500 kg/hr"` IS AN OPERATING WINDOW, NOT A SENSOR-VALIDITY RANGE. Cutting on it removes every furnace turndown and shutdown period. For a soft sensor trained on normal operation that may be exactly right; for a model expected to track transitions it destroys the only data those transitions live in. This is an engineering judgment, so the default must not be chosen silently — see openDecisions.

NO SERVER OPERATION MEANS 'MARK BAD / DROP ROW WHEN OUT OF RANGE'. Already recorded against DS-LAKE-005B-D-T01: cleaning_service.py's `clip` WINSORIZES (clamps the value, keeps the row) and `remove_outlier` REPLACES with mean/median — both are corrections, neither is the mark-Bad-then-impute or drop-row effect Step 3.1/3.2's own rule types (`action: 'mark' | 'drop'`) express. This feature inherits that same blocker; it is a server-side change in a parity-tested file, not a client translation layer.
TARGET HAS NO RANGE ENTRY. `target_y: "S204FBP.lab"` does not appear in features[] at all, so a range cutoff can never filter on the label column. Stated so nobody looks for it.

SAME TAG, TWO CONFIGS, TWO RANGES IS EXPECTED, NOT AN ANOMALY. One sheet holds several config_no entries, each with its own features[]. TI202.PV can legitimately carry a different range in config 1 and config 2. Precedent for the resolution shape exists (SD&TA preset cards already ship an OR/AND combine mode), but which mode is correct here is unresolved.
`parse_warnings[]` ALREADY EXISTS ON EVERY FEATURE AND IS EMPTY IN THIS PRESET. It is the natural home for a range-parse failure — reuse it rather than inventing a second warning channel.

THIS FEATURE EDITS THE SAME COMPONENT DS-LAKE-005B-D-T08a IS BLOCKED ON. `cutoff-section.tsx:153` is called only from `step-3-2-imputation.tsx:312`, and `data-cropping-chart.tsx` (CLIP_PRESETS / clipImpact) is T08a/T08b's own surface. Landing per-tag range rows while T08a's clipBasis fetch-path fork is still open risks two concurrent, conflicting edits. Sequence them, or resolve T08a first.

MARK-BAD ON AN OPEN-ENDED RANGE FABRICATES DATA, IT DOES NOT JUST LOSE IT. A tag reading 300 against '105-120 C' is a genuinely bad reading; imputing the hole is correct. But the sub-21500 values under '>21500 kg/hr' are REAL measurements of a real state (turndown/shutdown). Marking them Bad hands them to whatever fill step follows in that tag's pipeline, which replaces them with the mean of the surviving normal-operation flow -- the artifact then claims normal flow during a shutdown while the row keeps its real lab label. That is fabricated X against real Y; drop-row would only have LOST those rows, mark-Bad INVENTS them. With no fill step following, the Bad cell lands as frame_service.MISSING_VALUE=0.0 with status in the sibling column -- the 0.0-reads-as-a-measurement trap DS-LAKE-021 already records. The mark-Bad decision is NOT reopened (it is still right for the closed ranges that dominate the preset); ParsedRange.kind separates closed from lower/upper for free, and T05's UI now surfaces a dedicated warning for open-ended candidates rather than treating every shape identically.

THE BAND x EFFECT MATRIX IN cleaning_service.py HAS A REAL HOLE, JUST NOT ONE THIS FEATURE NEEDED TO FILL. crop=drop-outside, exclude=mark-inside(inclusive bounds) -- mark-outside is MISSING, and _op_exclude's inclusive <=/>= cannot substitute for it (a value exactly on a quoted bound would be wrongly marked Bad under per-tag precision rounding). Recorded for whoever eventually builds it; DS-LAKE-020 does not, because ConditionalRule already expresses the need client-side with correct STRICT semantics.

CONDITIONAL RULES -- HAND-TYPED, SD&TA-SOURCED, OR NOW PRESET-RANGE-SOURCED -- DO NOT REACH THE SERVER CLEAN PATH AT ALL. use-dataset-draft-pipeline.ts's applyClean/requestFinalPreview send only toCleaningOperations(cleaningPipelines[tag]) -- CleaningStep[], never conditionalRules/exclusions/valueCrop. The precleanse engine's server-side twin (cleaning_service.py:apply_fixture_case) raises NotImplementedError for anything but preprocessPipelines, so every precleanse-engine parity fixture is pytest.skip'd (test_parity.py's own skip branch). Consequence stated plainly so it is not discovered later as a 'defect': a range cutoff shapes the Step 3.2 client preview and the persisted recipe, but the SILVER artifact the server actually builds does not see it. Pre-existing, owned by DS-LAKE-005B-D-T01 -- this feature inherits it, does not introduce it.

REQUIRED_CASES IN test_parity.py OMITS crop_*/exclude_* ENTIRELY, EVEN THOUGH THE FIXTURES EXIST ON DISK. clip_both_bounds is required; crop_both_bounds/crop_low_only/crop_no_bounds_is_noop/exclude_both_bounds/exclude_high_only/exclude_no_bounds_is_noop are not, so the parity gate the ledger's own decisions.parity entry describes is thinner in practice than its description implies. Recorded, not fixed -- out of this feature's scope.

THE ENGINEERING UNIT DIES AT STEP 1 TODAY, INDEPENDENT OF THIS FEATURE. use-dataset-tag-metadata.ts's metaByTag is hook-local; Step 3 (raw-readings-table.tsx, tag-scatter-chart.tsx) fabricates units from a hardcoded 4-entry mock in lib/mock-readings.ts, so a real PI tag's unit renders as an empty string past Step 1. DS-LAKE-020-T03 fixes this only for its own consumer (the new dwTagUnitsAtom) and deliberately does NOT rewire the existing display components off the mock -- that is a real, separate, visible improvement outside this feature's scope (CLAUDE.md Section 3).
